summary.title: The benefits of note-taking by hand
summary.one_liner: Handwritten notes engage the brain through summarising and transforming information, which supports deeper understanding and memory better than verbatim laptop typing.
takeaways: Taking notes by hand is described as more cognitively engaging than keyboarding, because it involves summarising, paraphrasing and organising rather than verbatim copying.
The Cornell note-taking template, developed by education professor Walter Pauk, is named as a popular structured format for handwritten notes.
Fluency of hand (legibility plus speed), often through cursive, frees working memory for the demands of note-taking.
Sketching and drawing are presented as complementary ways to represent and deepen understanding of knowledge.
The article argues that keyboarding remains an important skill, so handwriting is a complement to digital tools rather than a total replacement.
summary.summary: This opinion piece, republished from The Conversation and written by education professor Hetty Roessingh, argues that handwritten notes benefit the brain more than laptop notes. It contrasts verbatim keyboard note-taking, called non-generative, with handwritten note-making, which involves summarising, paraphrasing and mapping concepts. The article also covers handwriting fluency in early grades, the Cornell template, sketching as a learning tool, and the continued appeal of paper journals. It cites examples such as Leonardo da Vinci and Florence Nightingale but offers little experimental detail.
